title: Hola — Your First Spanish Words
outcomes: Greet people in Spanish at any time of day
Say please, thank you, and excuse me
Tell someone you are learning Spanish

sections.content: Welcome to Spanish! By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to greet anyone, be polite, and — most importantly — tell them you're learning. This one phrase alone will change every interaction you have.

items: Greet people in Spanish at any time of day
Say please, thank you, and excuse me
Tell someone you are learning Spanish

sections.heading: Micro Grammar
sections.content: Spanish has formal (usted) and informal (tú) ways to say "you." At work and with strangers, use usted — it's always safe and respectful. "Disculpe" is the usted form of "excuse me." You don't need to memorize the rules yet — just know that the phrases in this course default to polite/formal, which is perfect for work.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: Morning at Kwik Trip — a Spanish-speaking customer walks in

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Hello! Good morning.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Good morning. Do you speak Spanish?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: I am learning Spanish.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Very good! Thank you.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: De nada. ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
lines.english: You're welcome. How can I help you?

breakdown.explanation: Do you speak Spanish? — A common question you'll hear. "Hablas" is the informal form.
Very good! — A common positive reaction. Muy = very, bien = good/well.
How can I help you? — Literally: "In what can I help you?" Standard customer service phrase.

questions.question: What does the employee tell the customer about their Spanish?
How does the customer react?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: It's morning. How do you greet a customer?
sections.feedback: ¡Perfecto! Buenos días is warm and professional — great for work.

turns.prompt: A customer says: "¡Hola!" — Greet them back and say good afternoon.
The customer asks: "¿Hablas español?" — Tell them you're learning.

questions.question: How do you say "Thank you" in Spanish?
Estoy _____ español.
Which greeting do you use in the evening?

sections.heading: Real-World Tip
sections.content: At Kwik Trip, you don't need to be perfect. A simple "¡Hola! Buenos días" with a smile shows respect and effort. Most Spanish-speaking customers will appreciate it enormously — even if that's all you say. And "Estoy aprendiendo español" is your safety net for any moment you feel lost.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: Hola = Hello (anytime)
Buenos días / Buenas tardes / Buenas noches for time-of-day
Por favor = Please, Gracias = Thank you, De nada = You're welcome
Disculpe = Excuse me (formal)
Estoy aprendiendo español = I am learning Spanish — your #1 phrase!

sections.content: Now that you can greet people, let's introduce yourself! Being able to share your name and ask for theirs turns a greeting into a real connection.

items.notes: Soy de Wisconsin, Soy de Estados Unidos

sections.heading: Micro Grammar
sections.content: "Me llamo" literally means "I call myself." It uses a reflexive verb — but don't worry about that yet. Just memorize the pattern: Me llamo + your name. For "I am from," we use "Soy de" + place. Soy means "I am" (permanent things like identity and origin).

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Hello! Good morning. My name is Simon.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: Mucho gusto, Simon. Me llamo María.
lines.english: Nice to meet you, Simon. My name is María.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Mucho gusto, María. ¿De dónde es usted?
lines.english: Nice to meet you, María. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: I'm from Mexico. And you?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: I'm from here, from Wisconsin.

breakdown.explanation: And you? — Short and casual. The customer switched to informal (tú) because you're becoming friendly.
I'm from here — "aquí" means "here." Simple and natural.

questions.question: Where is María from?
What does "Mucho gusto" mean?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: Introduce yourself. Say: My name is... (use your own name or Simon)
sections.feedback: ¡Muy bien! You just introduced yourself in Spanish.

turns.prompt: Someone says: "¿Cómo te llamas?" — Tell them your name.

questions.question: How do you ask someone's name formally?
_____ de Wisconsin.

sections.heading: Real-World Tip
sections.content: Learning a customer's name and using it next time they visit builds real connection. "¡Hola, María! ¿Cómo está?" — that alone can make someone's day. You don't need to have a full conversation yet. Names matter.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: Me llamo... = My name is...
¿Cómo se llama usted? = What is your name? (formal)
Mucho gusto = Nice to meet you / Igualmente = Likewise
Soy de... = I am from...
Using someone's name builds connection

title: Please, Thank You, and Sorry
outcomes: Use courtesy phrases in multiple contexts
Say sorry and excuse me appropriately
Sound polite even with limited Spanish

sections.content: Courtesy is the backbone of good communication — especially when your Spanish is still growing. Saying "por favor" and "gracias" covers a LOT of ground. This lesson goes deeper into polite language that makes every interaction smoother.

items: Use courtesy phrases in multiple contexts
Say sorry and excuse me appropriately
Sound polite even with limited Spanish

items.notes: Can go at start or end of any request
To get attention or apologize lightly

sections.heading: Micro Grammar
sections.content: "Por favor" can go at the beginning or end of a sentence — both are correct. "Un café, por favor" or "Por favor, un café." "Lo siento" is for real apologies. "Disculpe" and "Perdón" are lighter — use them to get attention, excuse yourself, or for small mistakes. At work, "Disculpe" is your go-to.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: You accidentally bump into a customer while stocking shelves

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Excuse me! I'm sorry.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: No se preocupe. No hay problema.
lines.english: Don't worry. No problem.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Thank you. Can I help you with something?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: Sí, ¿dónde está la leche, por favor?
lines.english: Yes, where is the milk, please?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: It's over there. In the back.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: With pleasure.

breakdown.explanation: No problem — literally "there is no problem." Very common and friendly.
Can I help you with something? — "algo" means "something."
In the back — useful for giving directions inside a store.

questions.question: Why does the employee say "Lo siento"?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer thanks you for your help. How do you respond warmly?
sections.feedback: ¡Excelente! Any of these responses sounds warm and professional.

turns.prompt: You need to get a customer's attention. What do you say?
A customer says "Gracias" after you help them. Respond.

questions.question: Which phrase means "I'm sorry" (for a real apology)?
"Con mucho gusto" means:

sections.heading: Real-World Tip
sections.content: At Kwik Trip, "Con mucho gusto" after helping someone sounds warm and professional. It's more personal than "De nada" and customers notice the effort. Even if you can't answer their question in Spanish, a polite "Disculpe, un momento por favor" while you find someone who can — that's great customer service.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: Por favor at start or end of requests
Gracias / Muchas gracias for thanking
De nada or Con mucho gusto for "you're welcome"
Lo siento for real apologies, Disculpe/Perdón for lighter ones
No se preocupe = Don't worry

title: Yes, No, I Don't Understand
outcomes: Say you don't understand and ask for help
Ask someone to repeat or slow down

sections.content: When a customer speaks fast and you catch nothing — what do you do? This lesson gives you the survival tools to stay calm, communicate honestly, and keep the interaction going. These are some of the most important phrases you'll learn.

items: Say you don't understand and ask for help
Ask someone to repeat or slow down

sections.heading: Micro Grammar
sections.content: "¿Puede...?" means "Can you...?" (formal). It starts many polite requests: ¿Puede repetir? (Can you repeat?) ¿Puede hablar más despacio? (Can you speak more slowly?) You'll use this pattern constantly. "Más" means "more" — más despacio = more slowly.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: A customer asks you something quickly and you don't catch it

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: Disculpe, ¿dónde puedo encontrar las baterías para el carro?
lines.english: Excuse me, where can I find car batteries?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Perdón, no entendí. ¿Puede hablar más despacio?
lines.english: Sorry, I didn't understand. Can you speak more slowly?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Yes, of course. Where... are... the batteries?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Ah, ¿baterías? No sé... Un momento, por favor.
lines.english: Ah, batteries? I don't know... One moment, please.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Yes, thank you.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Disculpe, estoy aprendiendo español. Voy a buscar a alguien que le pueda ayudar.
lines.english: Excuse me, I'm learning Spanish. I'm going to find someone who can help you.

breakdown.explanation: I didn't understand — past tense of "no entiendo." More specific than "no entiendo" because it refers to what they just said.
Yes, of course — A very common, friendly response to requests.
I'm going to find someone — "Voy a" = I'm going to. A useful preview of a pattern you'll learn later.

questions.question: What does the employee ask the customer to do?
What does the employee do when they can't answer?
options: Goes to find someone who can help

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer speaks too fast. Ask them to speak more slowly.
sections.feedback: ¡Perfecto! This one phrase will save you constantly.

turns.prompt: A customer asks you something you don't understand. What do you say?
You need a moment to figure something out. What do you say?

questions.question: "¿Puede repetir?" means:
No _____, ¿puede hablar más despacio?

sections.heading: Real-World Tip
sections.content: Here's the truth: saying "No entiendo" is NOT failure. It's communication. You're telling someone exactly what you need — and that takes courage. Native speakers are almost always happy to slow down or repeat. The worst thing you can do is freeze and say nothing. "No entiendo, ¿puede repetir?" keeps the conversation alive.

phrases.english: Can you speak more slowly, please?

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: Sí / No for basic confirmation
No entiendo = I don't understand (present) / No entendí (past)
¿Puede repetir? = Can you repeat?
¿Puede hablar más despacio? = Can you speak more slowly?
Un momento, por favor = buys you time
Saying "I don't understand" is communication, not failure

title: Putting It All Together
outcomes: Combine greetings, introductions, and courtesy in one flow
Handle a full basic interaction from start to finish

sections.content: You've learned greetings, introductions, courtesy, and survival phrases. Now let's put them all together into real interactions. This lesson is about flow — connecting what you know into natural conversations.

items: Combine greetings, introductions, and courtesy in one flow
Handle a full basic interaction from start to finish

sections.heading: Micro Grammar
sections.content: "¿Algo más?" literally means "Something more?" — use it after helping a customer with one request to check if they need anything else. "Que tenga un buen día" uses the subjunctive (don't worry about that yet) — just memorize it as a set phrase. It's the perfect way to end an interaction.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: A complete customer interaction at Kwik Trip — afternoon shift

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: ¡Hola! Buenas tardes. ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
lines.english: Hello! Good afternoon. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Good afternoon. Where is the coffee?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Está por allá, a la derecha.
lines.english: It's over there, to the right.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Thank you. And... do you have cream?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Sorry, I didn't understand. Can you repeat?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Cream. For the coffee.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: ¡Ah, sí! Está al lado del café.
lines.english: Oh, yes! It's next to the coffee.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Perfect. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: With pleasure. Anything else?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: No, that's everything. Thanks.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Have a good day.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Likewise. See you later!

breakdown.phrase: Está por allá, a la derecha
breakdown.explanation: It's over there, to the right. You'll learn more directions later — for now, "por allá" (over there) + pointing works great.
Do you have cream? — "Tienen" = you (plural/formal) have. Common customer question.
Next to the coffee. "Al lado de" = next to. Useful for store directions.
That's everything. — A common way customers say they're done.

questions.question: What does the customer ask for first?
What does the employee do when they don't understand?
options: Says sorry and asks them to repeat

questions.question: How does the employee end the interaction?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer just finished. Wish them a good day.
sections.feedback: ¡Perfecto! A warm goodbye leaves a great impression.

turns.prompt: A customer walks in during the afternoon. Greet them and offer help.
acceptableAnswers: hola buenas tardes en qué le puedo ayudar
buenas tardes, ¿en qué le puedo ayudar?
hola, buenas tardes. ¿en qué le puedo ayudar?
turns.hint: Greeting + How can I help you?

turns.prompt: They ask for something you don't understand. What do you say?
acceptableAnswers: disculpe no entiendo puede repetir por favor
turns.hint: Sorry, I didn't understand. Can you repeat?

turns.prompt: They say "Muchas gracias" as they leave. Respond and say goodbye.
acceptableAnswers: con mucho gusto que tenga un buen día
de nada que tenga un buen día
turns.hint: You're welcome + Have a good day!

questions.question: "¿Algo más?" means:
What's the best way to end a customer interaction?

sections.heading: Real-World Tip
sections.content: Here's your Unit 1 interaction formula: (1) Greet, (2) Offer help, (3) Try to understand, (4) If lost — say so and ask to repeat, (5) Help if you can, (6) Ask if they need anything else, (7) Wish them a good day. That's it. That flow works for every customer, every time. You already know every phrase you need.

phrases.spanish: Estoy aprendiendo español, pero quiero ayudarle.
phrases.english: I'm learning Spanish, but I want to help you.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: Full interaction flow: Greet → Help → Understand → Recover → Close
¿En qué le puedo ayudar? = How can I help you?
¿Algo más? = Anything else?
Que tenga un buen día = Have a good day
Hasta luego = See you later
You now have everything for basic customer interactions!
